Article Title: 'Police whose job is to provide security is making women feel threatened': Priyanka Gandhi on Jantar Mantar incident
Article Text:
Priyanka Gandhi raises women safety issue with an X post

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra on Sunday raised allegations of sexual harassment made by women journalists during reporting at Jantar Mantar, questioning the police response to the complaints.In a post on X, Gandhi said women journalists had accused police personnel of sexual harassment while covering the protests. She alleged that despite protests by several journalists, no FIR had been registered and no concrete action had been taken.Gandhi also claimed that women participating in peaceful protests had alleged “indecent” behaviour by police personnel.“The very police whose job it is to provide security is making women feel threatened,” Gandhi said, adding that women, from college students to journalists, were facing insecurity.Addressing Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah, Gandhi asked whether such treatment of women was appropriate and urged them to take notice of the allegations."From college students to journalists—women are facing insecurity everywhere. @narendramodi ji, @AmitShah ji, is this the right way to treat women? If not, then why don't you take notice of it?" she wrote in an X post.The Delhi Police had earlier said that three female journalists made allegations of sexual harassment during the protest in the New Delhi area on October 3. The complaints were received by the New Delhi district police and transferred to the Crime Branch at Kamla Market for further action.
Article Summary: Priyanka gandhi raises women safety issue with an x post on sunday. She alleged that despite protests by several journalists, no fir had been registered. Gandhi also claimed that women participating in peaceful protests had alleged “indecent’ behaviour by police personnel.

Article Title: ‘She will continue’: Thiruvananthapuram mayor denies BJP councillor Sreelekha resigned from post
Article Text:
Rajesh had initially said he received a resignation letter from Sreelekha on September 30.

Mayor says Sreelekha will remain councillor

CPM attacks BJP councillor

Sreelekha's role in BJP

Thiruvananthapuram Mayor V V Rajesh on Sunday said former Kerala DGP and BJP councillor R Sreelekha would continue in office, denying that she had resigned from the Corporation.The controversy began after a message purportedly posted by Sreelekha in a WhatsApp group of residents in her ward said she had submitted her resignation to the Mayor and would give a copy to the District Collector on October 5.Rajesh had initially said he received a resignation letter from Sreelekha on September 30 but had not sent it to the Corporation Secretary, who is authorised to accept such resignations. He had also said the letter cited personal difficulties.On Sunday, however, Rajesh said there was no resignation letter."Who told you that she has given the resignation letter? She will continue and I have said it yesterday itself," he said.When asked about the WhatsApp message attributed to Sreelekha, Rajesh did not directly address it. He instead said there was no threat to the functioning of the Corporation."You want the governance to take place smoothly. As all desire, the governance will go forward strongly," he said.Rajesh said councillors often submit letters seeking funds for their wards or raising issues related to their functioning."Such a letter was given to me for the smooth operations in the ward. As she is a ruling councillor, I find that some of the matters cited in it require the party's intervention. Some have to be done by the Mayor. We will address the matters as in letters given by other councillors," he said.He said Sreelekha would remain a councillor and complete her five-year term.Sreelekha has not yet publicly responded to the conflicting statements over her alleged resignation.CPM leader and former minister V Sivankutty criticised Sreelekha and questioned her credibility."Nothing that Sreelekha says can be believed. Not only that, she will resort to any threat to secure position and power. This should only be viewed as a threat directed at the BJP to gain new positions," he said.Asked whether Sreelekha was putting pressure on the BJP with a possible move towards the Congress, Sivankutty said some politicians would move wherever they saw greater benefits."Naturally, some go where there is greater benefit. They will move to wherever they get the maximum advantage," he said.The BJP took control of the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation for the first time last year after securing the support of 51 councillors, including an Independent, in the 101-member civic body.Sreelekha was elected from the Sasthamangalam ward on a BJP ticket in last year's local body elections. She is currently the BJP's state vice president.Her continuation as a BJP councillor is significant for the party because its majority in the Corporation is narrow and depends on the support of an Independent councillor.Sreelekha also contested the Vattiyoorkavu Assembly seat in April but lost to Congress leader K Muraleedharan.
Article Summary: Rajesh had initially said he received a resignation letter from sreelekha on september 30. He had also said the letter cited personal difficulties. On sunday, however, rajesh said there was no resignation letter. "who told you that she has given the resignation letter? She will continue," he said.

Article Title: AAP holds protest after 3 women journalists allege sexual harassment by cops - key points
Article Text:
The complaints were received by the New Delhi district police following the protest on October 3

What the journalists alleged

Dipke's allegations, Rahul Gandhi's attack

NEW DELHI: Three women journalists have alleged sexual harassment by police personnel while covering a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar on October 3, with the complaints now transferred to the Crime Branch for a “fair and impartial enquiry”. The allegations have drawn criticism from journalists and opposition leaders, with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CJP) set to protest over the incident.AAP Delhi unit chief Saurabh Bharadwaj and party workers staged protests in front of Parliament Street police station, demanding registration of an FIR.The complaints were received by the New Delhi district police following the protest, during which police personnel were deployed to maintain law and order. Delhi Police said the complaints against police officers were being transferred to the Crime Branch, Kamla Market, which will examine the allegations and record statements of the complainants and other people concerned.The allegations have also triggered wider questions over the treatment of journalists and protesters during the demonstrations. CJP has announced a protest following the allegations, while journalist Dipke hit out at Delhi Police on X, alleging that the force had also picked up people who had no connection with CJP and tried to link them to the organisation to establish a foreign-funding angle.One of the journalists told PTI that an assistant commissioner of police sexually assaulted her while she was covering the protest. She alleged that police personnel were detaining protesters and that no women police personnel were present at the spot."Police personnel were detaining protesters, and there were no women police personnel present at the spot. I asked ACP Vivek Bhagat of the Delhi Police about the absence of women police personnel, following which he sexually assaulted me and pushed me back," she alleged.The journalist said she and others subsequently went to a police station to lodge an FIR but alleged that no action had been taken so far. Delhi Police, however, said on Sunday that complaints had been received from three women journalists alleging sexual harassment by police personnel."On 03-10-26, during the protest in New Delhi area, while being in law and order situation, allegations of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists against police officers. New Delhi District has received their complaints," Delhi Police informed on X.Dipke alleged that Delhi Police had also detained people who had nothing to do with CJP and tried to establish a foreign-funding connection."Delhi Police has also picked up a couple of people who had nothing to do with CJP and tried to forcibly link them to CJP to establish a foreign-funding angle. A friend just told me that one of them was brutally beaten by Delhi Police and has also lost his job because of the arrest," Dipke wrote on X.The Press Council of India expressed “shock and dismay” over the treatment of journalists and urged Delhi Police to immediately act on the complaint.Rahul Gandhi also accused Delhi Police of misconduct at Jantar Mantar and questioned Union home minister Amit Shah over the alleged treatment of journalists and protesters.The protests were held against CEC Gyanesh Kumar amid demonstrations over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Delhi Police detained several protesters, while at least three FIRs were registered in connection with the mass protest held near Jantar Mantar on October 2.
Article Summary: Three women journalists have alleged sexual harassment by police personnel while covering a protest at jantar mantar on october 3. Delhi police said the complaints against police officers were being transferred to the crime branch, kamla market.

Article Title: No room to roam: The cost of a crowded planet for wild animals
Article Text:
What shrinking habitats do to India's wildlife

A shrinking home, not a vanishing one

Not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life

The cost to people

Where space is being rebuilt

What the evidence points to

Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out

Over the past fifty years, the average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent, according to WWF's Living Planet Report 2024. The report names loss and degradation of habitat as the most commonly reported threat, driven mainly by how the world grows its food.This finding raises a plain question. When animals lose the land, water and forest they depend on, what happens to them?Habitat rarely disappears all at once. It is cut into pieces by farms, roads, canals, railway lines, power lines and growing towns. Each piece may still have trees and water, but it supports fewer animals than the original whole did.The 73 per cent figure also needs careful reading. It describes the average change across thousands of monitored populations. It does not mean that three-quarters of the world's animals are gone, or that three-quarters of species have disappeared. What it does show is a steady thinning, and the report describes such declines as an early warning of greater risk to species and ecosystems. The pressure it describes is gradual and widespread rather than the result of a single event, which is partly why it is easy to overlook. The report also notes that some populations have held steady or recovered where conservation has worked.“This is not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life,” said Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF.The effects usually arrive in a recognisable order. Food and water become harder to find, so animals travel farther to reach them. Their routes cross fields, highways and railway tracks. Animals with large ranges, such as elephants and big cats, are affected first, because they need the most room.Smaller populations face a slower problem. When forest patches are cut off from one another, animals cannot move between them to find mates. Over time a small, isolated group becomes more vulnerable to disease and to sudden shocks such as drought or fire. Wherever forest meets farmland or settlement, animals and people also meet more often, and not always safely.India's elephants show how this plays out. The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants, according to the last census in 2017. Most of them do not live inside protected areas. Government and press figures put the share outside reserves at about 80 per cent. That share matters for everything that follows. A herd that lives mostly outside reserves has no boundary between it and the land that people farm, travel across and build on.For these herds, a journey between feeding grounds can pass through paddy fields, village lanes, rail lines and overhead power cables. Official data tabled in Parliament in 2024 shows what that means. Over five years, the leading cause of unnatural elephant deaths was electrocution, ahead of train accidents, poaching and poisoning. Odisha, Assam, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu reported the largest numbers of electrocution deaths.The government has taken some steps in response. It has identified and ground-validated about 150 elephant corridors, the routes herds use to move between forests. The Railways and Environment ministries have also formed a standing committee to reduce deaths on tracks.Tigers tell a more hopeful story, with a warning attached. The 2022 estimate counted at least 3,682 tigers in India, a record, spread across 53 tiger reserves. These reserves are among the best protected forests in the country.But the same assessment shows the limits of protection. Roughly a third of the reserves need stronger protection, habitat restoration or more prey for the tigers to feed on. A few reserves in Mizoram, Nagaland and Jharkhand reported almost no tigers at all. Summaries of the report also describe many reserves as small islands of forest, joined to one another by a limited number of corridors. A reserve with a healthy tiger population can send young animals out in search of territory of their own, and many of them end up in unprotected land among farms and villages.The record count and the weak reserves belong in the same account. Protection works where it is applied well, and the gaps appear where it is not.Kaziranga's protection does not stop at the park boundary, and a new proposal from the Assam government has put that line under debate. The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve with a site-specific zone of one to three kilometres. An ESZ is a regulatory buffer, declared by the environment ministry on a state's proposal. It is not an outright ban: depending on the notification, activities in it may be prohibited, regulated or permitted, and mining is among those most strictly restricted.Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma says the 10-km limit applies only because Kaziranga has not yet been finally notified. He argues it brings populated areas such as Kaliabor, Doboka and Jakhalabandha under restrictions, and holds up civic projects like a proposed stadium in Bokakhat. The state says the park's boundary and its UNESCO World Heritage status will not change, and that the 10-km zone stays in force until a new one is notified. Some residents agree. Hundreds rallied in support of the proposal on August 18, saying the current limits get in the way of building homes and basic infrastructure.The opposition and conservationists are not convinced. Congress state president Gaurav Gogoi led a protest at the Kohora range and alleged that the change could give legal cover to mining. The state government rejects the charge. Conservationists such as Jadav Payeng and Kavita Ashok point to the annual floods, when rhinos, deer and elephants move to higher ground outside the park. A smaller zone, they warn, could cut off those routes.A 2025 conservation assessment notes that a smaller zone is not necessarily a weaker one if it is designed to protect the most sensitive areas. Whether it does will depend on the final notification, which will decide whether wildlife corridors, flood escape routes and wetlands fall inside the line.Space does not only mean forest. Globally, freshwater species have seen the steepest declines in the WWF report, and wetlands are often among the first places to be drained or built over.The report points to Chennai, where rapid urban growth has led to a large loss of wetland area. Wetlands shelter birds, fish and amphibians, and they also soak up floodwater for the city around them. When they go, wildlife loses a home and people lose a buffer.When space runs out, people pay too. Government data tabled in Parliament showed that elephants killed 2,853 people in India over five years, with the highest toll in 2023. Many of these deaths happened in places where farms, villages and elephant routes overlap. The elephant deaths and the human deaths come from the same stretches of land, where both now depend on the same ground.The Environment Ministry has issued guidelines on managing human-elephant conflict, and it says compensation is provided for losses. These measures respond to the damage after it happens. They do not by themselves restore the space that animals have lost.Some efforts aim at the cause. West Bengal has begun a community programme called Gajamitra, or Friends of Elephants, in which local people take part in reducing conflict. Conservation scientists have also suggested low-cost methods for farmers, such as planting chillies, ginger or citrus around fields, which elephants tend to avoid, or placing beehives along field edges.The WWF report also records progress in India, where it says some wildlife populations have stabilised or recovered. It credits government initiatives, careful habitat management, scientific monitoring and community involvement. At the global level, the report calls for more effective conservation along with changes in food, energy and finance systems.The picture from India and from the world is consistent. Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out, they wander into danger, they come into conflict with people, or they disappear from places they once held. Where land is protected, connected and shared with the people who live beside it, some populations hold their ground or recover.India's own examples point in both directions: electrocutions and train deaths on one side, a record tiger count and recovering populations on the other. The difference lies largely in whether land is protected and linked together, and whether the people who live beside wildlife are part of the plan.The question on World Wildlife Day is how much room is left for wildlife, and who decides what happens to it.
Article Summary: India holds about 60 per cent of the world's asian elephants. The average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent. Loss and degradation of habitat is the most commonly reported threat. A third of the reserves need stronger protection, habitat restoration or more prey for the tigers to feed on.

Article Title: CJP protest: Scuffle breaks out near Shiv Sena Bhavan as supporters return from stir; watch
Article Text:
A scuffle erupted near Shiv Sena Bhavan in Dadar after a protest





MUMBAI: A scuffle broke out near Shiv Sena Bhavan in Dadar after supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) returned from a protest at Shivaji Park.A video from the spot shows protesters arguing, with some allegedly hitting each other.The situation soon turned physical, prompting police to intervene and disperse those involved. Mumbai Police later said the situation was under control and peaceful.The incident followed a CJP protest at Shivaji Park over the party’s demands concerning Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Before the protest, a Dadar resident had opposed the demonstration. “They are doing it forcefully. This protest should not take place,” the resident said, adding that such demonstrations disturb peace in the area.The CJP has been demanding Kumar’s resignation and changes to the functioning and appointment process of the Election Commission. The Election Commission currently lists Gyanesh Kumar as the Chief Election Commissioner.Mumbai Police had earlier denied permission for the CJP to hold its October 2 protest at Shivaji Park. The party later announced a “Jail Bharo Andolan”.Meanwhile, a 75-year-old Thane resident died after suffering a heart attack while attending the CJP protest at Shivaji Park on Friday evening.The deceased was identified as Gopalakrishna Subbaiya Pillai, a resident of Dosti West County in Thane.Pillai arrived at Shivaji Park around 4.30pm to attend the protest. Around 5pm, he complained of chest pain. His friend and police personnel at the spot helped take him to Sushrusha Hospital in Shivaji Park.Police personnel tried to revive him with CPR before he was taken to the hospital, where he died while undergoing treatment. Police said doctors attributed his death to a heart attack.
Article Summary: A scuffle broke out near shiv sena bhavan in dadar after supporters of the cockroach janta party (cjp) returned from a protest at shivaji park. The situation soon turned physical, prompting police to intervene and disperse those involved. Mumbai police later said the situation was under control and peaceful.

Article Title: Of 97 left out in Goa, 88 are back, 3 others are Portuguese citizens: EC
Article Text:
Goans born before 1961 in former Portuguese territories, as well as their kids and grandchildren, can apply for a Portuguese passport based on a citizen card issued by the Portuguese authorities after verifying their birth/descent documents.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The office of the Goa chief electoral officer on Thursday said 88 of the 97 voters in the state whose names could not be included in the roll due to an alleged ECINet issue have been added back after their duly filled Form 6 was accepted. However, he also revealed that three of these 97 electors are Portuguese passport holders while six others were electors currently based outside India."In respect of voters who are currently residing outside India, officials are making efforts to establish and maintain contact with them for necessary action," the CEO said while sharing the status report on the 97 cases on X.Section 9 of the Constitution disallows dual citizenship. Goans born before 1961 in former Portuguese territories, as well as their kids and grandchildren, can apply for a Portuguese passport based on a citizen card issued by the Portuguese authorities after verifying their birth/descent documents. Portugal recognises dual citizenship; however, since dual citizenship is not allowed in India, anybody who acquires a foreign passport must surrender his Indian passport.As per Sec 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a person's Indian citizenship automatically ceases upon acquiring foreign citizenship.Thus, three of the Portuguese passport holders in Goa may be classified as non-citizens, making them ineligible to be enrolled as Indian electors, said a source.Incidentally, Portuguese passport holders form 3% of the cohort of 97 electors for which the Goa CEO had repeatedly written to the EC after the ERO could not add them back via ERONet, leading the ECs to also raise questions on why access for such changes was 'centralised' and not available to the field officers. The issue was further amplified by the opposition parties after The Indian Express reported on the alleged internal notes of the election commissioners in this regard.EC sources on Thursday said the due diligence by the ERO the second time around may have served the purpose of SIR, as it is aimed at eliminating ineligible persons from the voters' list. Also, the fact that the issue was detected at the ERO level proves that the absolute right to add or delete a voter, based on verification, remains with the field officers, an EC officer told TOI.
Article Summary: 88 of the 97 voters in the state whose names could not be included in the roll due to an alleged ecinet issue have been added back. Three of these 97 electors are portuguese passport holders while six others were electors currently based outside india.

Article Title: Delhi riots case: High court rejects bail pleas Of Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam
Article Text:
Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam denied bail by high court

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has refused to grant bail to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the UAPA case related to the 2020 Delhi riots.Senior Advocate Trideep Pais, appearing for Umar Khalid, submitted that there had been three “small changes in circumstances” since the earlier proceedings. He also referred the court to a Supreme Court judgment in support of his submissions.Pais pointed out that charges have not yet been framed in the case and, consequently, prosecution witnesses are yet to be examined. The court also noted that the charges were yet to be framed.Pais further submitted that a Special Leave Petition (SLP) is pending before the Supreme Court and that the trial court has indicated it would await the Supreme Court’s order. He then continued his submissions by referring to the Supreme Court judgment.Khalid and Imam had approached the Delhi High Court earlier this year after their bail applications were dismissed by the trial court for the third time on July 4. Imam was arrested in the case on August 25, 2020, while Khalid was arrested on September 13, 2020.The Delhi Police has opposed their bail pleas in the high court, asserting that the two were “masterminds” of the riots, PTI reported.The police argued that they could not seek bail on parity with other co-accused, stating that the Supreme Court had earlier categorised them as being part of the “command authority” and held that their “risk profiles” justified “continuing detention”.The police also argued that the present bail pleas were in the teeth of the Supreme Court’s January 5 order, which directed them to seek release only after the examination of protected witnesses was completed or after one year, whichever was earlier.On July 4, the trial court rejected Khalid’s bail application, saying it had “no option but to follow” the Supreme Court’s January 5 order and could therefore neither entertain the plea nor grant him relief.On September 2, 2025, a Delhi High Court division bench denied bail to Khalid and Imam. The Supreme Court upheld the verdict on January 5 but granted relief to co-accused Gulfisha Fatima, Meeran Haider, Shifa Ur Rehman, Mohammad Saleem Khan and Shadab Ahmad.A bench of Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice NV Anjaria had observed that there was a prima facie case against Khalid and Imam under the UAPA.On May 22, the Supreme Court granted six months’ interim bail to co-accused Abdul Khalid Saifi and Tasleem Ahmad, while referring to a larger bench the issue of prolonged incarceration of undertrials under the UAPA due to the stringent conditions for granting bail.
Article Summary: Umar khalid, sharjeel imam denied bail by high court in uapa case related to 2020 delhi riots. Delhi police has opposed their bail pleas in the high court, asserting that the two were ‘masterminds’ of the riots.

Article Title: 'AAP asked you not to': Congress leader claims CJP refused party's help during Assam detention

Congress, CJP spar over Assam outreach

NEW DELHI: Congress spokesperson Reetam Singh has claimed that Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka refused to meet Congress leaders during his recent Assam visit. He alleged that the group was told to stay away because its outreach was "an Aam Aadmi Party initiative".Singh's response came after Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das called out a fake "liberal ecosystem", saying that they believed they were alone responsible for “saving India, saving constitution”. However, they did not name Congress directly.Singh made the allegation in a post on X on Saturday while responding to Ranka, who had criticised what he described as an “entire ‘self-declared liberal’ ecosystem” targeting CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.Singh said Congress workers had helped CJP members after they were detained by Assam Police and claimed that Ranka nevertheless declined a courtesy meeting with Congress leaders, including Assam Congress president Gaurav Gogoi.This comes days after Ranka and more than 40 CJP volunteers were detained in Guwahati ahead of a regional volunteers' meeting. Opposition parties, including Congress, AAP, the Assam Jatiya Parishad and Raijor Dal, had criticised the police action.Addressing Ranka, Singh said Congress members had helped secure the release of CJP workers after their detention.“When you were detained by Assam Police. We, Congress people helped to get CJP people out. Yet you categorically refused to have even a courtesy meeting with our Congress leaders and Gaurav Sir,” Singh said."You refused it because the Aam Aadmi Party asked you to not to. Kunki Chowdhury who was your Host in Guwahati, was on Election Campaign with AJP President Lurin Gogoi Da for a Congress Candidate in Nagaon. Even they had asked you to meet and discuss with Congress. Yet not once, you chose to engage with Congress or our students wing. You asked us to stay out of it. And that it is a Aam Aadmi Party initiative," he added.Singh also referred to Kunki Chowdhury, at whose residence Ranka and other CJP members were reportedly detained. He claimed Chowdhury had asked Ranka to meet Congress leaders and discuss the group's activities.CJP members had been detained from the residence of Assam Jatiya Parishad leader Kunki Chowdhury in the Dispur area ahead of their scheduled meeting.Singh further accused Ranka and CJP of trying to portray the movement as an AAP initiative and referred to the group's earlier protests in Delhi.“We know how you sidelined Neha Bora in the Jantar Mantar 1.0 protests and when even Left chose to engage with our Leader Rahul Gandhi Ji. You decided you will not engage under direct instructions of Arvind Kejriwal,” he said.He also alleged that AAP had previously sought to associate itself with movements led by others, citing the India Against Corruption movement and activist Sonam Wangchuk's protest.“Aam Aadmi Party is known for piggy riding and hijacking issues of others,” Singh said.Singh said CJP was “a people's movement” and argued that it should not be treated as the property of any political party.“Let us keep it civil and issue centric. The cause is bigger than a political party,” he said.“CJP is a decentralised movement. There is no one Supreme Leader or his hierarchy. We all are equals. That is why people support it.”Ranka's post that triggered Singh's response had accused a “self-declared liberal” group of targeting Dipke and questioning his growing reach.“An entire “self-declared liberal” ecosystem has been activated to denounce @abhijeet_dipke and the fact that he has been able to capture the imagination of millions of Indians after a LONG LONG time,” Ranka said.CJP co-convenor Saurav Das also criticised what he described as a group from outside the BJP that believed it alone was responsible for “saving India, saving constitution”. Neither Ranka nor Das named a political party in their posts."It’s a very big problem. A certain section—not just the BJP—another party thinks “saving India, saving constitution” is only their job. They are self-declared liberals and self-declared thekedars of the constitution," he said."It’s a very salty ecosystem, acting worse than the BJP’s ecosystem sometimes. They must realise that they can’t divide and rule through such tactics. Their massive failures over the years has led us to this moment where the young have to show the way. So they should just zip it on us and focus on how to support the young! Total buffoons!" he added.The latest exchange has brought CJP's political affiliations and its relationship with opposition parties into focus, even as the organisation continues its outreach on issues including education and electoral rolls.
Article Summary: Congress, cjp spar over assam outreach. Congress spokesperson reetam singh claims cockroach janta party (cjp) co-convenor ashutosh ranka refused to meet congress leaders during his recent assam visit. He alleged that the group was told to stay away because its outreach was "an aam aadmi party initiative" ranka's post that triggered singh's response had accused a “self-declared liberal” group of targeting dipke.

JAMMU: A 19-year-old woman from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) was intercepted by Army personnel after she crossed the LoC in J&K’s Rajouri district, officials said Saturday.Nothing incriminating was found with Samiya Azeem when she was caught late Friday, the officials said, adding she is a resident of PoK’s Kotli district. “During preliminary interrogation, the girl maintained she had inadvertently crossed the LoC and entered Indian territory,” an official said.Troops found Samiya in the border village of Pukherni in Rajouri’s Nowshera sector. He was handed over to Pakistan Army personnel a week later at Chakan Da Bagh border post after checks and other formalities.Abdul Hussain, a 70-year-old from Lehari Khurd village in Pakistan, was intercepted in Indian territory on March 25 this year and sent back within six hours after it was established that he had entered inadvertently.

Article Title: Congress resets Team Uttar Pradesh: 5 clear messages for BJP and Akhilesh Yadav
Article Text:
Congress replaced Ajay Rai with Aradhana Misra Mona as Uttar Pradesh Congress chief.

1. A bigger, but amicable, say at seat-sharing table

What Mona Misra said after her appointment as UP Congress chief

2. Rebuilding old social reach, but with a new mix

What Ajay Rai said after being replaced as UP Congress chief

3. Not conceding Muslim vote

What Imran Masood said after UP Congress organizational reshuffle

4. Congress wants credibility

5. Women power at heart

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Congress has overhauled its Uttar Pradesh organisation ahead of the 2027 assembly election, replacing Ajay Rai with three-time Rampur Khas MLA Aradhana Misra Mona as state unit president and appointing Saharanpur MP Imran Masood as working president. The party has also named Chaudhary Virendra Singh as Congress legislature party leader.The reshuffle brings together a prominent Brahmin leader from eastern UP, a Muslim leader with influence in western UP, and Dalit and OBC representation in senior organisational positions. Rajendra Pal Gautam, a Dalit leader, is already the party's Uttar Pradesh in-charge. With these recent appointments, Congress may be trying to widen its social and regional reach after years of electoral decline in the state.Taken together, the appointments suggest that Congress is trying to do two things at once: strengthen its bargaining position with the Samajwadi Party while rebuilding an independent political identity in Uttar Pradesh.The timing is important. The 2024 Lok Sabha election revived Congress's presence in UP through its alliance with Akhilesh Yadav . But Akhilesh’s party remains the much larger organisation in the state. In the 2024 polls, SP moved 32 seats up and won 37 seats, registering a 15.73% gain in vote share.On the other hand, Congress also slightly improved its Lok Sabha tally with 6 seats and a jump of a little over 3% vote share.Congress is now trying to turn that electoral revival into a more substantial organisational base before the 2027 assembly election in a state which has been long associated with Congress's political success story.Here are the five messages embedded in the reset.The appointment of Aradhana Misra Mona as UPCC president, along with the elevation of Imran Masood, suggests that Congress wants to push for a larger share of assembly seats while keeping its relationship with the Samajwadi Party workable.Masood has been unusually vocal about Congress' seat demand. On September 3, he argued that if Congress' electoral performance continued to improve, its share of seats should also increase."Hum koi bhikhari hain jo Samajwadi Party se bheekh mangenge? ... Party formula tay karegi, lekin jo formula Lok Sabha election mein tha, woh formula nahi hoga. (Are we beggars who will beg from Samajwadi Party? ... The party will decide the formula, but it will not be the same formula used in the Lok Sabha elections)," he had told ANI.Congress' UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam has also spoken of seeking an equal number of seats with the SP, while Masood has backed a 50:50 formula.The rhetoric sharpened on September 28, when Masood directly declared: "If Akhilesh Yadav is unhappy (with seat-sharing discussion), the loss will be his own... We fail to understand what the anger is even about."Mona's elevation, on the other hand, sends a somewhat different signal. Unlike the more combative rhetoric around seat-sharing, her appointment gives Congress a state president who is seen as having a more workable equation with the SP leadership. Her political experience and close association with the Congress leadership also give her a role in managing the alliance even as the party pushes for greater space.The numbers give Congress some basis for making that argument. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the SP won 37 of UP's 80 seats while Congress won six, taking the INDIA bloc's combined tally to 43. The SP's 37-seat tally was a dramatic rise from five seats in 2019.However, going by the numbers, Congress cannot negotiate from the position of higher power and will most likely have to settle for the junior partner role.But how "small" the partner role it gets will be crucial.One of the clearest messages in the new team is social and regional balancing.Mona is a prominent Brahmin face from eastern Uttar Pradesh. Masood brings a prominent Muslim face from western UP. Devinder Nishad gives the organisation an OBC, riverine-community face, while Alok Prasad brings Dalit representation into the senior state team. Rajendra Pal Gautam is already the party's Dalit in-charge for Uttar Pradesh.The choice of Mona is particularly significant because she replaces Ajay Rai, a Bhumihar leader, with another upper-caste leader from a different community. The switch from Rai to Mona could be read as an attempt to reconnect with Brahmin voters who were traditionally associated with Congress but have, over time, moved substantially towards the BJP.This rejig comes at a time when the upper-caste groups (Rajputs, Brahmins, Tyagis) reportedly feel increasingly sidelined by BJP's aggressive outreach toward non-Yadav OBC and Dalit vote banks. Tensions stem from ticket distribution cuts, perceived administrative favour toward Rajputs over Brahmins, and farmers' issues.Mona's appointment, however, is not simply a return to Congress's old social formula. The new team combines upper-caste, Muslim, Dalit and OBC representation, while also distributing the leadership geographically between eastern and western UP.The BJP has built a broad social coalition of its own in Uttar Pradesh. Congress' organisational response now appears to be an attempt to create multiple social entry points into the party rather than rely on a single caste or community bloc.Masood's elevation carries another particularly important message for western Uttar Pradesh.The Saharanpur MP is one of Congress' most prominent Muslim leaders in the state, and his appointment puts a western UP Muslim face in the second-most important position in the state organisation. His appointment seems to be a direct attempt to attract and consolidate Muslim support.That matters because the SP has traditionally been the principal opposition party competing for the Muslim vote in UP. The 2024 Lok Sabha election demonstrated the strength of that relationship.A post-election CSDS-Lokniti analysis estimated that 77% of Muslim respondents in Uttar Pradesh voted for the SP and 15% for Congress, while 2% reported voting for the BJP. These are, of course, survey estimates and not absolute vote counts. However, it may reflect the trend.The actual election results also showed the importance of Muslim-heavy constituencies to the opposition's performance. Congress won Saharanpur and Sitapur, while the SP and its allies captured several other such seats.Masood's promotion therefore gives Congress a prominent vehicle to seek Muslim support directly rather than relying entirely on the SP to bring that constituency into the alliance.Mona's appointment is significant because she brings an electoral record to the top of the state unit.She first entered the Uttar Pradesh assembly through a bypoll in 2014 and subsequently retained Rampur Khas in the 2017 and 2022 elections. She has therefore won the seat three times. Before entering the assembly, she served as block pramukh of Sangramgarh from 2002 to 2014 and held positions in the organisation and cooperative sector.Her 2022 victory was particularly notable because Congress was reduced to just two assembly seats across Uttar Pradesh. She defeated BJP's Nagesh Pratap Singh by 14,741 votes, polling 84,334 votes, or 50.27%, according to Election Commission data.That gives Congress a state president who is not merely an organisational appointee but an incumbent with a repeated assembly-winning record.The appointment of Aradhana Misra Mona also gives Congress a prominent woman at the helm of its Uttar Pradesh organisation, at a time when BJP too is putting renewed emphasis on its women leaders in the state.The timing is notable. The BJP has recently brought back Smriti Irani into a more prominent organisational role, signalling that women leaders continue to have an important place in its political strategy. Irani, who beat Rahul Gandhi and represented Amethi in the Lok Sabha from 2019 to 2024, remains one of the BJP's most recognisable women faces in Uttar Pradesh.The Mona-Priyanka Gandhi combination will give Congress a big women power picture it can easily put on its posters.The wider electoral numbers also underline why women matter. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the Election Commission recorded female voter turnout in Uttar Pradesh at 57.22%, compared with 56.46% among men. Women therefore turned out at a slightly higher rate than men in the state.As a bonus, Mona's elevation also gives Congress a combination of representation and political substance: a woman leader, a Brahmin face, a three-time assembly winner and someone with an established organisational network.The new UP team combines experience with caste, community, regional and gender representation, giving Congress multiple entry points in the voter base. The real test now will be whether the reshuffle can translate into stronger grassroots organisation and enough bargaining power ahead of the 2027 assembly election.
Article Summary: Congress replaced ajay rai with aradhana misra mona as uttar pradesh congress chief. With these recent appointments, congress may be trying to widen its social and regional reach after years of electoral decline in the state. Mona is a prominent brahmin face from eastern uttar pradesh.

Article Title: Helicopters, influencers and nail art: The money trail of 2026 assembly elections
Article Text:
The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns.

The campaign war chests

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that higher campaign spending guarantees electoral success? Yes, it often leads to victory No, spending doesn't always equal success 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Different states, different stakes

A statewise representation of poll expenditure by the BJP and Congress.

Ads, aircraft and the spending gap

The funding gap between BJP and Congress, and where the money was spent.

From nail art to AI calls

When spending and seats diverged

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From paying social-media influencers to allocating money for 'nail art', the BJP 's expenditure statements reveal the range of campaign activities funded during its bid to win the West Bengal assembly election. A closer look at political parties' filings with the Election Commission of India (ECI) makes for interesting reading, revealing how spending priorities varied according to the political stakes in different states. However, the TVK example is only a humbling reminder that in democracy, greater outreach may lead to greater eyeballs, but it is no guarantee for success.The BJP declared Rs 529.39 crore expense for this year's assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Congress declared Rs 248.55 crore as spending, less than half that amount.A TOI analysis of the expenditure filings shows that Rs 178.78 crore of the Rs 280.84-crore difference, nearly two-thirds, came from advertisements and travel by star campaigners, the top leaders a party sends around a state to address rallies. Money given directly to candidates accounted for only Rs 16.27 crore of the gap. At least on paper, the BJP's extensive advertising campaigns and deployment of senior leaders, many of them massive crowd pullers, distinguished its expenditure pattern from that of Congress.The BJP won 207 seats in West Bengal in the results declared on May 4 and later won the Falta repoll to take its tally to 208. It formed its first government in the state, ending the Trinamool Congress's 15-year rule. TMC chief Mamata Banerjee lost her own seat, Bhabanipur, to the BJP's Suvendu Adhikari. The BJP-led NDA won Assam for a third consecutive term, while the NDA led by the All India NR Congress retained Puducherry.In Keralam, the Congress-led UDF returned to power after 10 years. Congress won 63 of the 140 seats, the CPI(M)-led LDF 35 and the BJP three. In Tamil Nadu, film star Vijay's TVK, contesting its first assembly election on the whistle symbol, won 108 of the 234 seats, ahead of the DMK with 59 and the AIADMK with 47. Subsequently, Vijay became chief minister.The BJP, Congress and CPI(M) filed accounts covering all five elections, with the CPI(M) declaring only Rs 39.04 crore as expenditure. The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore spending for Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore expenses in a statement covering Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Keralam.TVK reported Rs 19.81 crore for Tamil Nadu, according to TOI report. TMC's full 2026 expenditure statement is not available on the ECI website.Political parties have no overall election expenditure ceiling, but individual candidates face spending limits. The accounts can also include expenditure authorised but not yet paid. The BJP's Bengal return, for instance, recorded Rs 89.32 crore in outstanding general-campaign expenditure at the end of the election period.More than half the BJP's money, Rs 286.99 crore or 54.2 per cent, went to Bengal, followed by Rs 96.27 crore in Assam. Together, the two states accounted for Rs 383.26 crore, or 72.4 per cent of the party's total. The BJP also declared Rs 82.67 crore in Keralam, Rs 51.56 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.90 crore in Puducherry.The spending pattern broadly reflected the different political stakes.The figure broadly aligns with what was at stake too. BJP was desperate to get power in Bengal after catapulting to second position in 2021 and sensing anti-incumbency was heavily weighing down on Mamata Banerjee. In Assam, it was looking to consolidate a strong position. The party had much less at stake in Tamil Nadu where it is still an emerging force. In Keralam, a much smaller state than Tamil Nadu, more amount was pumped in sensing an opportunity to break the binary nature of the state politics.For Congress, the situation was totally different. Its biggest chance for coming to power was in Keralam and it’s no surprise that the party spent the most in Keralam, Rs 105.34 crore or 42.4 per cent of its total, followed by Assam at Rs 67.62 crore, or 27.2 per cent. It declared Rs 42.08 crore in Bengal, Rs 22.25 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.25 crore in Puducherry.Bengal accounts for most of the gap between the two parties, perhaps unsurprisingly, although both parties were contesting almost the same number of seats in the state. The BJP declared Rs 244.91 crore more than Congress there, about 87 per cent of the total difference. Keralam was the only state where Congress declared more, by Rs 22.67 crore.Party filings divide spending into different categories, and three of them help explain the BJP–Congress difference to an extent.The BJP declared Rs 187.54 crore on general-party media advertisements, which promote the party as a whole rather than individual candidates. Congress declared Rs 92.52 crore, a difference of Rs 95.02 crore.Star-campaigner travel covers trips by a party's senior leaders, and the BJP's schedules list aircraft and helicopter travel for several of them. The BJP declared Rs 106.25 crore under this head against Congress's Rs 22.49 crore, about 4.7 times as much and Rs 83.76 crore more.Direct grants, the money a party transfers to candidates, were much closer. The BJP declared Rs 111.79 crore and Congress Rs 95.52 crore, a difference of Rs 16.27 crore, with the BJP's grants about 17 per cent higher. Congress spent slightly more on grants than on general-party media advertisements.In Bengal, the BJP recorded grants of Rs 20 lakh each to its 294 candidates, totalling Rs 58.80 crore. In the same state, it declared Rs 88.48 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 52.18 crore on star-campaigner travel.Grants, however, are only part of the support candidates receive, since parties also pay centrally for publicity, rallies and other campaign activities.The difference extended beyond advertisements and star campaigners' travel. The BJP declared ₹52.34 crore on publicity materials, including posters, banners and flags, against Congress's ₹11.48 crore. Under other general-party expenses, the BJP recorded ₹48.83 crore against Congress's ₹6.78 crore, another ₹42.05-crore gap. Congress, however, declared more expenditure on general-party meetings and rallies, ₹7.99 crore against the BJP's ₹4.06 crore.The filings name the people and firms that were paid, though they do not always specify what services were delivered.In Bengal, the BJP's accounts include payments recorded against social-media influencers and content creators. TOI earlier reported that influencer Sayak Chakraborty acknowledged receiving Rs 2.5 lakh for two videos, The Bengal accounts also contain entries for nail art. Four entries of Rs 1 lakh each, marked "Nail Art", appear under public meetings and rallies. Another Rs 9.65 lakh is recorded against Visionary Edge for a "Nail Art Prog" under media advertisements.Sayak was not the only influencer or content creator named in the accounts. Others have also acknowledged receiving payments. Yet the separate virtual-campaign schedules recorded no expenditure.Across the five elections, the BJP's accounts list Rs 41.83 crore against Google India and Rs 15.65 crore against Facebook India Online Services, a total of Rs 57.48 crore, of which Rs 31.39 crore was attributed to Bengal. This amount is already included in the BJP's advertising expenditure. Advertising purchased through agencies for social media may also appear under other names.The filings also point to the use of artificial intelligence in election outreach. Congress's headquarters recorded Rs 3.72 crore against Neomarq Flare Solution LLP in Assam for a service described as "AI 2 Way Voice Calling".In Tamil Nadu, the DMK's Rs 197.85 crore included Rs 70.63 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 45.75 crore in grants to candidates. Five entries marked "Social media" added up to Rs 16.87 crore, naming Vipras Ads, Ravi Publicity Services, Glovy Trading and Populus Empowerment Network.Populus appeared four times in the accounts, for manpower and consultancy, campaign production, digital advertising (Rs 6.37 crore) and social media. Together, these entries totalled Rs 74.94 crore, about 37.9 per cent of the DMK's expenditure.The AIADMK recorded Rs 103.99 crore of its Rs 112.40 crore, or 92.5 per cent, in a single entry for Pramanya Strategy Consulting, described as "Social Media Promotion, TV, Website". Because the filing does not break down this amount, it cannot be compared directly with the DMK's specifically labelled social-media entries.The CPI(M)'s Keralam unit accounted for Rs 28.60 crore of the party's Rs 39.04 crore, and its Bengal unit Rs 8.23 crore. In Keralam, the party recorded Rs 19.53 crore on general-party media advertisements, of which Rs 18.77 crore, about 96 per cent, appeared in four entries naming Maitri Advertising for print, television and electronic media.These entries identify the companies named in the expenditure schedules, not necessarily the ultimate media outlets or platforms.The BJP won Bengal, the state where it declared its largest expenditure, while the Congress-led UDF won Keralam, where Congress spent the most.Tamil Nadu, however, presented a striking contrast.TVK reported expenditure of Rs 19.81 crore, including about Rs 6.3 crore on media advertisements, Rs 3.5 crore on Vijay's air travel and Rs 2.1 crore on public meetings and roadshows, according to TOI's September 26 report.The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore in a statement covering three jurisdictions. Although the reporting coverage differed, TVK's declared expenditure was substantially smaller than that of either established Dravidian party.Yet TVK won 108 assembly seats, compared with the DMK's 59 and the AIADMK's 47.Vijay entered politics with a considerable advantage in public recognition, having spent decades as one of Tamil cinema's biggest stars. His existing fan base and celebrity appeal may have given TVK organic visibility, yet the difference in spendings can’t be ignored.The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns, from helicopters and digital advertisements to influencers, consultants and AI-powered calls. They also expose the limits of pumping funds to win elections. Hence Tamil Nadu perhaps had the most important lesson for mainstream political parties.
Article Summary: The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns. The bjp declared rs 529.39 crore expense for this year's assembly elections in west bengal, assam, keralam, tamil nadu and puducherry. Congress declared rs 248.55 crore as spending, less than half that amount.

Article Title: Teaching is just the start: The crushing burden on India's college teachers
Article Text:
According to a survey on higher education, while recommended student-teacher ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.

Modern classroom: More than academics

When attendance collide with career

Teacher becomes institutional buffer

When personal problems enter classroom

Counselling gap, a stigma problem

Emotional burden on teachers

Beyond the classroom

In a brightly lit classroom at an engineering college in Bengaluru, a fourth-year Computer Science lecture is underway. At the front, a professor moves through a technical lesson while also keeping track of attendance sheets and administrative requirements.In the middle rows, a student sits quietly, mentally calculating train schedules between Bengaluru and Pune. He is trying to work out how to explain to a corporate employer that a career-launching Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) could be at risk because of a mandatory offline attendance requirement for a single elective subject.The scene captures a growing tension inside India’s higher education system.For final-year students, college is no longer only about completing a degree. With competition for jobs intensifying, students are increasingly focused on internships, practical skills, early employment and mental health support. But the institutional framework around them remains tied to attendance thresholds, credit requirements, standardised evaluation and administrative compliance.Caught at the centre of these competing pressures is the college teacher.According to data from the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), while recommended Student-Teacher Ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.In public and state institutions, that figure can rise to 35:1 or 50:1, with individual undergraduate lectures accommodating 80 to 120 or more students per section.The pressure is compounded by faculty shortages. Central universities report faculty vacancy rates between 29% and 34%, while senior professor vacancies frequently exceed 50%. Across technical institutions such as the IITs, NITs and IIITs, unfilled positions range from 30% to over 50%.This leaves teachers performing several roles at once: academic instructors, institutional policy enforcers, career advisers and, often, informal listeners when students are struggling.At the same time, they have to manage UGC Academic Performance Indicators, NAAC and NIRF documentation and heavy teaching loads.For today's students, particularly those in their final year, the classroom is closely linked to the question of what happens after graduation.“A student may come because he is confused about an internship, worried about placements or simply doesn't know how to deal with something happening at home. We try to listen, but there is a limit to what a subject teacher can realistically handle,” Prakash, a college faculty member at an engineering college, says.From the student's perspective, the final year can feel like a race against time, with academic requirements running alongside internships, placements and preparations for entering the workforce.Pranav Vats, a final-year Computer Science and Engineering student in Bengaluru, describes what students prioritise:“Whenever a guy comes to a college, he eventually wants to get placed. He doesn't want to get a 9-plus CGPA every semester. He just wants to get placed in a good company and do well in his career financially and also growth-wise... I have been doing internships from the first year itself. And whatever interviews I have been going through, nobody asked me about what my CGPA is. Everybody just asked, okay, how much do you know, how much practical skills you have, and how well you understand the market and how well do you understand your business in which you are going to work now. ”That shift creates a difficult balance for teachers. Students may see practical experience as more directly connected to employment, while faculty members remain responsible for ensuring that students complete prescribed courses, credits and attendance requirements.The tension becomes particularly visible during placement and internship season.Pranav describes a situation in which he had secured an internship opportunity in Pune after clearing an interview:“Two, three months back, I got an interview. I've cleared it. I went to Pune. And at that time, I got permission from college. They gave me this letter of acknowledgement that you can go and pursue your six months internship, and all. But all of a sudden, after two months, they are saying that no, you have to fulfil your academic requirements and all... This company is very good. I'm doing very well there. And they are giving me the PPO for it. I could have got placed. But right now, this company is not giving away. College is saying that you have to attend weekly once class. As a student, it is not possible for me to come from Pune to Bangalore every week to attend some stupid class that is not even relevant to my coursework, which is not even relevant to my computer science degree... It is just an open elective subject.”He says discussions with his mentor, department head and other authorities did not resolve the problem. Pranav says similar situations have affected other students, including those with jobs or internships in Bengaluru itself.He says, “A guy got placed in Bangalore itself. And he said, ‘Sir, I can't attend this class this week because I've got placed.’ They said, ‘You have to fulfill this academic thing’.”For teachers, however, understanding the student's situation does not necessarily mean being able to change the rule.“The final year is particularly difficult because everything seems to happen at once. Students are completing projects, dealing with attendance and examinations, and at the same time worrying about placements and what they are going to do after graduation. You can see that pressure building up, especially when a student's plans don't work out,” the faculty said.The faculty member explains the dilemma, “There are situations where a student gets an internship or an opportunity outside the college and genuinely needs flexibility. As a teacher, you may understand why that opportunity matters to him. But you are also responsible for implementing the academic requirements. That can put the teacher in an uncomfortable position because you may sympathise with the student without having the authority to change the rule. ”The teacher is therefore often caught between three sets of expectations.The administration expects attendance, syllabus completion and documentation for institutional requirements. Students expect empathy, career guidance and flexibility. Parents expect academic performance, safety and career outcomes.The teacher may have to explain an institutional decision to a student without having any authority over that decision.“Sometimes the student is upset with the institution, the parents are worried about the student's performance and the department is concerned about academic requirements,” the teacher explains. “The teacher ends up sitting in the middle. We are expected to explain one side to the other, even though we may not have control over the decision ourselves.”For students, this can reinforce the perception that teachers are primarily there to enforce attendance and award marks.Pranav puts it bluntly, “They don't care, they just want these things to attend classes, they want attendance, they want marks, that's it... If you go to an off-campus thing, where majorly everybody is applying right now, nobody asks you about your CGPA. They just want you to have your practical skills. But this CGPA thing or whatever coursework they are teaching us in college, it is not even relevant to what we will work in our offices. ”The pressure is not limited to academics and placements.Teachers are also increasingly expected to recognise when students are struggling emotionally, even though they may not be trained to provide professional mental health support.“You spend enough time with a class to notice changes,” the faculty member observes. “If a student who is normally interactive suddenly stops speaking, misses classes or stops submitting work, you notice it. The difficult part is deciding whether to ask, ‘Is everything okay?’ because you don't know whether the student wants you to enter that part of his life,” Prakash say.The teacher describes the boundary involved, “There is a very fine line between being concerned about a student and becoming intrusive. If I ask too many questions, it may seem intrusive. If I don't ask anything, I may miss something important. Teachers are constantly trying to judge where that line is.”At the same time, faculty members recognise their own limitations.“I want my students to know that they can approach me, but I also have to be honest about my limitations. I can listen, I can help them think through a problem and I can direct them towards the right person. But I am not trained to provide therapy, and pretending otherwise can be harmful,” Prakash says.Many institutions have counselling cells or mentor-mentee systems, but having a service does not necessarily mean students will use it.Pranav says his mentor-mentee system is largely focused on academic issues:“For every 20 or 30 sets of people there is assigned one mentor. So whatever the issues you have regarding the college, you can talk with them and they can get a resolution about it... [But] there is nothing like that through which we can discuss our career... They are strictly for the subject.”He says students also face peer pressure around seeking counselling.“We have one basically like they have hired a person... if you have any emotional issues or something like that, then you can go schedule a session,” Pranav says. “[But] if you suppose you go to a counsellor there is this peer pressure. If you go to a counselor, or maybe you're discussing things with the teacher, you would seem like a weak person.”“This thing is very very disturbing to the students and nobody talks about it because everybody feels that okay, if I talk about it I can feel weak about it and people will think that okay he's not mature enough to deal with his own problem on his own... I talk to some of my friends about it who are eventually on the same path... but majorly I work with my pressure on my own,” Pranav adds.When behaviour changes significantly, teachers also have to balance intervention with confidentiality.“If I feel that a student's behaviour has changed significantly, I cannot just say, ‘That's his personal matter.’ There are situations where you have to involve the appropriate support system. But you also have to be careful about confidentiality and about not turning a student's difficulty into a public issue,” Prakash says.While student stress receives increasing attention, the pressure on faculty can remain largely invisible.A teacher managing a class of 80 to 120 students may also have to deal with staff shortages, administrative work, evaluations, meetings and institutional documentation. A difficult conversation with a student does not necessarily end when the class does.The faculty member says teachers need institutional support if they are expected to take on these additional responsibilities.Prakash says, “I don't think teachers are unwilling to take on a larger role. Most teachers care about what happens to their students. But if the expectation is that we should identify emotional distress, provide career guidance, handle academic problems and support students through personal crises, then the institution also has to give teachers training and a proper support structure.”The experiences of both students and teachers point to a larger structural problem.When colleges rely on individual teachers to enforce academic rules, handle administrative requirements, guide students through careers and respond to emotional distress, the teacher becomes the point where multiple pressures meet.The solution therefore cannot rest entirely on individual faculty members.As colleges respond to changing job markets and rising student pressures, the system would require clearer boundaries for faculty responsibilities, greater flexibility for final-year students navigating legitimate career opportunities, and stronger professional support systems.For the teacher standing at the front of the classroom, the challenge is no longer simply teaching the subject. It is managing everything that happens around it, often without the authority, time or institutional support required to do so.
Article Summary: According to a survey on higher education, recommended student-teacher ratio (str) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1. In public and state institutions, that figure can rise to 35:1 or 50:1, with individual undergraduate lectures accommodating 80 to 120 students per section.

Article Title: Agra court grants bail to 6 Cong workers arrested for defacing CEC Gyanesh Kumar's ancestral home

NEW DELHI: A local court on Saturday granted bail to six Congress workers arrested for allegedly defacing the outer wall of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's ancestral home in Agra during a protest against alleged manipulation of voter lists.The accused - Mukesh Dhangar, Anil Yadav, Rajesh Kumar, Manoj Gaur, Rajesh Gautam and Pankaj Chaudhary - were granted bail after furnishing surety bonds of Rs 20,000 each, advocate Santosh Dixit, who represented them, said.The six were arrested on September 29 and had been sent to jail following a case registered against them under several provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including those relating to attempt to murder, rioting, wrongful restraint and assault or criminal force against a public servant.Dixit said the police had dropped Section 109(2) of the BNS, relating to attempt to murder, after failing to substantiate the charge in its submissions before the court.In an earlier hearing, the court had directed the police to conduct a detailed investigation into the invocation of Section 109(1), asking them to specify the facts, injuries, medical evidence, eyewitness testimony or other evidence supporting the charge.The court had also directed the investigating officer to complete the probe by October 3 and drop the section if the investigation did not establish the alleged offence.On September 28 protest in which some Congress workers allegedly wrote slogans with black paint on the gate and outer wall of Kumar's residence in the Vijay Nagar area of Agra.Police registered the case at Hariparvat police station on a complaint by a sub-inspector against eight named persons and 15-20 unidentified Congress workers.The other charges in the case include Section 121 of the BNS, relating to voluntarily causing grievous hurt to deter a public servant from performing his duty, Section 126 on wrongful restraint and Section 132 on assault or criminal force against a public servant. Provisions relating to rioting, house-trespass, criminal intimidation and intentional insult were also invoked.Congress Agra city president Amit Singh welcomed the bail order and said the party would continue its agitation against Kumar."The serious section imposed by the police has been removed by the court. This is a victory for democracy," Singh said, adding that the Congress would continue its campaign until Kumar resigns as Chief Election Commissioner.
Article Summary: Court grants bail to six congress workers arrested for allegedly defacing outer wall of chief election commissioner gyanesh kumar's ancestral home in agra. The six were arrested on september 29 and had been sent to jail following a case registered against them under several provisions of the bharatiya nyaya sanhita.

Article Title: Drug addicts turn to painkillers amid Nasha Mukt crackdown in J&K
Article Text:
(Representative image): Investigations have so far led to the recovery of 2,19,425 tablets and capsules of pharmaceutical drugs, as well as 3.830 kg of codeine-containing liquid, including the storage containers, police said.
